flashcards.front: RA 8792 Sec. 8: how is a retention requirement met electronically?

flashcards.back: The statute and the reliability context; authenticity can still be challenged.
flashcards.front: RA 8792 Sec. 9: what determines evidentiary weight?

flashcards.back: The document is the record; the signature is the identify-and-approve function. Each has its own functional-equivalence rule (Secs. 6 vs. 7).
flashcards.front: Electronic document vs. electronic signature — why keep them distinct?

flashcards.back: (1) Is it legally recognized? (2) Are its contents admissible/authentic? (3) Was accessing, disclosing, or using it lawful (Secs. 31–32)? Recognition is not a presumption of truth.
flashcards.front: An e-record exists. What three questions must still be separated?

flashcards.back: Authenticity, integrity, source, custody, and reliability under the Rules on Electronic Evidence — a record is not self-proving.
flashcards.front: What must the proponent of an electronic record establish?

flashcards.back: Statutory or contractual receipt — not technical delivery to a server, and not when a human opened the message. Check whether the addressee designated a system and the place-of-business rules.
flashcards.front: Dispatch vs. receipt vs. reading: what controls contract formation?

flashcards.front: “Email sent” — is the offer accepted?

flashcards.front: RA 8792 Secs. 25–26 and government use: what is the test?

flashcards.front: Sec. 9(b)(1): what are the general deadlines?

provisions.citation: Republic Act No. 8792 (Electronic Commerce Act of 2000), Sections 1-5
provisions.explanation: Title, policy, objectives, application and definitions. Sec. 4 applies to data messages and electronic documents used in commercial and noncommercial activities, including domestic and international dealings, subject to statutory exclusions and other laws. The defined terms (data message, electronic document, electronic signature, originator, addressee, information system, intermediary, service provider) are distinct and not interchangeable.

provisions.citation: Republic Act No. 8792 (Electronic Commerce Act of 2000), Section 6
provisions.explanation: Functional equivalence for writing: information is not denied legal effect, validity or enforceability solely because it is in electronic data message or electronic document form. An electronic document satisfies a writing requirement when the statutory accessibility and reliability criteria are met, centered on remaining accessible for subsequent reference with integrity safeguards.

provisions.citation: Republic Act No. 8792 (Electronic Commerce Act of 2000), Section 7
provisions.explanation: Legal recognition of electronic signatures turns on the statutory requirements: an electronic signature can identify the person and indicate approval when the applicable conditions are met. A typed name, scanned image or login is not automatically sufficient; assess reliability, intent, attribution and the relevant transaction.

provisions.citation: Republic Act No. 8792 (Electronic Commerce Act of 2000), Section 8
provisions.explanation: A retention requirement can be met electronically when the information remains accessible for later reference and the statutory conditions are satisfied, including the required form and related origin, destination and time information where applicable.

provisions.citation: Republic Act No. 8792 (Electronic Commerce Act of 2000), Section 9
provisions.explanation: Evidentiary weight and presumptions depend on the statute and the reliability context; authenticity of an electronic document can still be challenged.

provisions.citation: Republic Act No. 8792 (Electronic Commerce Act of 2000), Sections 31-32
provisions.explanation: Confidentiality and lawful access. Separate (1) whether the record is legally recognized, (2) whether its contents are admissible and authentic, and (3) whether accessing, disclosing or using it is lawful. A valid electronic document can be unlawfully obtained, and a lawfully accessed message can still fail authentication.

provisions.citation: Republic Act No. 8792 (Electronic Commerce Act of 2000), Sections 16-24
provisions.explanation: Communication of electronic documents: dispatch and receipt rules, including the designated versus non-designated information system distinction, and the statutory rules for place of dispatch and receipt and the parties' place of business. Ordinary contract formation under Civil Code Arts. 1318-1326 (definite offer, absolute acceptance, consent, object, cause) still applies; negotiation, advertisement or automated acknowledgement is not automatically acceptance.

sourceRefs.excerptHint: Dispatch, receipt, time and place; contract formation

provisions.citation: Republic Act No. 8792 (Electronic Commerce Act of 2000), Sections 25-26
provisions.explanation: Electronic communication applied to carriage of goods and related actions and documents: paper-record functions such as information about goods, instructions, delivery, receipt or transfer of rights are tested against functional-equivalence conditions.

provisions.articleOrSection: Secs. 17-29 (government use; syllabus range as given by the reviewer)
provisions.citation: Republic Act No. 8792 (Electronic Commerce Act of 2000), government-transaction provisions
provisions.explanation: Governmental use of electronic documents and transactions. Recognition provisions facilitate electronic filing and processing, but the agency's valid rules, technical standards, required identity checks, statutory filing deadlines and special form requirements remain important. The reviewer cites the broad range Secs. 17-29 without mapping individual sections; verify the exact section against the statutory text.

provisions.citation: Republic Act No. 8792 (Electronic Commerce Act of 2000), Section 33
provisions.explanation: Penalties for specified unlawful acts. Identify the prohibited act in exact statutory language, the actor, any required mental state, the statutory penalty and related liability under other applicable law. Distinguish authentication failure from unauthorized access or hacking, and contract noncompliance from a criminally prohibited act; check amendments and related cybercrime, data privacy, evidence, consumer and financial-sector laws where raised.

provisions.citation: Republic Act No. 11032 (Ease of Doing Business and Efficient Government Service Delivery Act of 2018), Sections 3-4
provisions.explanation: Covered government offices and agencies, including LGUs, GOCCs and other government instrumentalities providing business- and nonbusiness-related transactions, whether in the Philippines or abroad. Sec. 4 definitions are exam material: simple transaction (ministerial action or inconsequential issues), complex transaction (evaluation of complicated issues), highly technical application (requires technical knowledge, specialized skill or training), processing time (receipt of complete application with documents and payment through issuance of approval or disapproval), red tape, BOSS, fixer, and business-related versus nonbusiness transactions.

provisions.citation: Republic Act No. 11032 (Ease of Doing Business and Efficient Government Service Delivery Act of 2018), Sections 5-8
provisions.explanation: Institutional duties: re-engineer systems and procedures, publish a Citizen's Charter, implement a zero-contact policy subject to lawful exceptions, and hold the head of office responsible for compliance. The Charter is an operating commitment listing requirements, procedure, responsible person or office, processing time, fees, filing and payment modes, and complaint or redress mechanism; offices may not demand beyond the charter or applicable law, and the head's responsibility is distinct from the processing officer's duties and ARTA oversight.

provisions.citation: Republic Act No. 11032 (Ease of Doing Business and Efficient Government Service Delivery Act of 2018), Section 9
provisions.explanation: General processing-time deadlines in Sec. 9(b)(1): simple 3 working days, complex 7 working days, highly technical 20 working days, subject to periods otherwise provided by law and lawful extension rules. Time runs from receipt of the complete application with required documents and payment; compute working days, check holidays and agency-specific periods, and know the statutory ground, maximum extension and notice requirements from the current text.

provisions.citation: Republic Act No. 11032 (Ease of Doing Business and Efficient Government Service Delivery Act of 2018), Section 10
provisions.explanation: Automatic-approval mechanism for covered applications where the office fails to act within the prescribed period, conditioned on complete submissions and required fees, plus an automatic-extension concept for qualifying renewals. Not every silence means approval: establish coverage, completeness, deadline expiration, the kind of application, and statutory exceptions or procedures.

provisions.citation: Republic Act No. 11032 (Ease of Doing Business and Efficient Government Service Delivery Act of 2018), Sections 4(a) and 9
provisions.explanation: Adverse action should be a written, reasoned approval or disapproval recognized by Sec. 4(a), communicated within the period and under Sec. 9. Distinguish an actual written denial, with any required reasons, signer or authority, and appeal or review information, from mere inaction; vague oral discouragement is not automatically a valid statutory denial.

provisions.citation: Republic Act No. 11032 (Ease of Doing Business and Efficient Government Service Delivery Act of 2018), Sections 11-15
provisions.explanation: Streamlined procedures for local licences and related fire safety clearances and certificates, the Business One Stop Shop (single common site or portal for LGU business permit applications, payments and approvals), barangay-specific procedure, the Central Business Portal, Philippine Business Registry and database infrastructure, and interconnectivity. City or municipality applications follow separate rules from barangay applications; FSEC and FSIC are streamlined but technical review is not eliminated; digital infrastructure does not abolish substantive requirements.

provisions.citation: Republic Act No. 11032 (Ease of Doing Business and Efficient Government Service Delivery Act of 2018), Sections 16-19
provisions.explanation: Roles for the Civil Service Commission's anti-red-tape work, the Anti-Red Tape Authority (ARTA), and the Ease of Doing Business and Anti-Red Tape Advisory Council. A complaint referred or investigated through the oversight route is distinct from a private action challenging a specific permit denial.

provisions.citation: Republic Act No. 11032 (Ease of Doing Business and Efficient Government Service Delivery Act of 2018), Sections 21-23 and 25
provisions.explanation: Violations and penalties, with Sec. 25 addressing immunity in the statutory context. Use the exact prohibited act (refusal to accept a complete application, failure to act within the timeline, imposing extra requirements, failing to issue a receipt, collusion with a fixer, or other distinct conduct). Separate administrative, civil and criminal consequences with the responsible person, mental state, penalty range and proceeding; delay alone does not prove a violation. A fixer includes an outsider with access to government personnel; official employment is not always required.
